01.r: A man of another people, not an Israelite.
01.n: Gesenius: strange, of another country and people, foreign; as a noun, a foreigner. This is a different word from the sojourner who lives in Israel, so our English keeps 'foreigner' for it.

02.r: Interest is permitted on a loan to a foreigner.
02.n: The causative form of the verb behind the noun 'interest', as in Deuteronomy 23:19 on this page: 'make (him) pay interest'. Gesenius gives the first sense as TO BITE. The imperfect here grants a permission, 'you may'.

03.r: A fellow Israelite, set against the foreigner.
03.n: The Hebrew has only 'and'; the contrast comes from setting the two clauses side by side, so English needs 'but'.

05.r: The same act, forbidden toward a fellow Israelite.
t: thou shalt lend that which he wanteth ... usury
05.n: The Douay-Rheims follows the Latin Vulgate and turns the clause into a command to lend without usury.

06.r: Gives the purpose of the law.

07.r: God's blessing is tied to lending freely to a brother.
07.n: Gesenius puts 'to bend the knees, to kneel' first among this verb's senses, ahead of 'to bless'.

08.r: The personal name of Israel's God.

09.n: The form is plural but the meaning is singular.

10.r: No undertaking is left out of the blessing.

11.r: Whatever you reach out your hand to do.
11.n: BDB gives 'outstretching': 'the outstretching of your hand' is an idiom for whatever you undertake. Gesenius's entry gives a related form meaning a sending, and with 'hand', a thing upon which the hand is sent.

12.r: The hand you put to your work.

13.r: Where the work is done: on the land itself.
13.n: Literally 'on' or 'upon' the land; most translations say 'in'.

14.r: The land of Canaan, which Israel is about to enter.

15.r: Introduces the land Israel is entering.
15.n: Hebrew says 'which ... there', with 'there' later in the clause; together they mean 'into which'.

16.n: The pronoun is written out, which gives 'you' some emphasis.

17.r: Israel is on the point of going in.
17.n: A participle, 'you are going', of an action already under way. Gesenius gives the first sense as to come in, to enter.

18.r: Points to the land as the place of entry.
18.n: Literally 'thither', 'to there': it picks up 'that' earlier in the clause. The translations fold it into 'whither' or leave it out.

19.r: To take the land and hold it.
19.n: Gesenius gives the first sense as TO TAKE, TO TAKE POSSESSION OF, TO OCCUPY, especially by force, and argues that this, not 'to inherit', is the primary meaning.

01.n: ἀλλότριος, belonging to another, a stranger.

02.n: ἐκτοκίζω, to lend at interest, built on τόκος.

03.n: The Greek marks the contrast with δὲ, 'but'.

11.n: ἔργον, work: the Greek says 'in all your works'.

12.n: The Greek has only 'your' here; 'hand' is not rendered.

15.n: εἰς ἣν, 'into which'; our Greek text prints the relative as ἢν, a slip in the accent.

17.n: εἰσπορεύομαι, to go in; our Greek text prints it with a stray mark, εἰσπ·ορεύῃ.

18.n: ἐκεῖ, 'there': the Greek keeps the Hebrew's 'there'.

19.n: κληρονομέω, to inherit, to receive as one's lot: the Greek leans to 'inherit' where Gesenius takes the Hebrew as 'take possession'. Our Greek text prints the last word as ἀυτὴν, for αὐτὴν, 'it'.
